en: There is no self, yet there is rebirth; there is karma with its fruit, yet there is no agent;
there is no goer, yet there is a journey toward the auspicious; there is bondage, yet there is no bound one.
Even in such a profound mystery, the teaching of this Sage remains uncontradicted.

Homage to him, the speaker of what is right, whose glory shines among gods and men. I pay homage to the Buddha, the awakener, who is perfected with manifold virtues, who has uprooted the latent tendencies along with their roots, and who knows how to bring about the welfare of the world.
I bow to that Dharma which is the destruction of craving, secure, and inconceivable;
it is beloved by the Noble Ones, for from it fear arises in the foolish. [It is] equal to all-knowing wisdom... [and] brings about... 8.1.3.
I pay homage to that noble Saṅgha of immeasurable splendor who has entered the path;
[and] those of immeasurable splendor who always assert a self distinct from the body.
The pervasive, inactive, and unmanifest [Self] is for them nothing more than a mere word.
For nothing other than the body, the senses, and the intellect is perceived;
indeed, it is suffering that arises, and suffering alone that ceases.
For if the self were to exist, it would have to be either eternal or impermanent;
in both these cases, a great fault would necessarily follow.
If [the self] were indeed impermanent, there would be the futility of actions;
rebirth would not exist, and liberation would occur without effort.
Now,
if he were eternal and omnipresent, there would be neither end nor birth;
for space is pervasive and eternal, yet it neither passes away nor is it born.
If this self were omnipresent, yet not situated anywhere,
it would simultaneously be liberated both here and after death, and exist everywhere at once.
[The Buddha said: "In liberation, because this [self] is inactive due to its omnipresence, there can be no performance of actions. *Buddhacarita* 16.81.
And how could there be a connection with the fruit from actions that have not been performed?
Or, if he were the agent [of his own suffering], he would not inflict suffering upon himself. *Buddhacarita* 16.82.
For if there were independence, who indeed would inflict suffering upon themselves by themselves? Moreover, because the self is eternal, transformation would not be possible.
And when pleasure and pain are experienced, his transformation is observed. Through the attainment of knowledge and through the abandonment of the afflictions, liberation exists.
Therefore, for that which is inactive and all-pervading, even liberation does not exist.
For I consider the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) to be liberated even from the primary and secondary material causes (prakṛti-vikāra).
I consider it to have the nature of procreation and indeed the nature of a seed;
for even though the self is conceived as pure and liberated. (Buddhacarita 12.70)

Because the conditions for rebirth still exist, he will not be liberated. Just as a seed does not sprout due to the absence of the proper season, soil, and water, so too [does the seed of existence fail to grow].
Just as that [tree] grows through various conditions, so too, in my view, does he [the self] grow.
(8.1.17) Buddhacarita 12.72 Since liberation is conceived to result from the abandonment of karma, knowledge, and craving, [it follows that the self is not required].
The absolute abandonment of that [defilement] is not possible as long as the self exists.
(8.1.18) Having repeatedly abandoned these three, a distinction is indeed perceived. (Buddhacarita 12.73)
But wherever the self remains established, there these three are subtle;
and because of the subtlety of the faults here, as well as the non-activity of the mind.
Because his lifespan is long, liberation is postulated for him; and this abandonment of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) which is postulated—
As long as the self exists, there can be no abandonment of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
Furthermore, unless one is liberated from the Sāṃkhya categories and the like, this [self] does not become devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). *Buddhacarita* 12.76.

Therefore, in the absence of the absence of qualities (*nairguṇya*), liberation is not ordained for him. For there exists no separation between the possessor of qualities and the qualities themselves.

For fire is not perceived when separated from form and heat. Likewise, before the body there would be no possessor of the body, and similarly, before the qualities there would be no possessor of the qualities.
Therefore, having been liberated at first, that embodied being is bound again. Whether the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is separated from the body, he must be either a knower or indeed ignorant.

If there is a knower, he must have an object of knowledge; as long as there is an object of knowledge, one is not liberated. Therefore, it is established for you that there is no knower; what is the use of this imagined self?
For even without a self, ignorance is well-established, like that of wood or a wall;
therefore, because it does not exist, the self cannot be designated as "this."
Nor does it exist as a cause, for it performs no action at all;
it is not manifested by its effects, nor indeed is it produced by anyone.
Since such an unreal thing has been described, therefore the self does not exist.
This other [argument] is also highly praised as an illuminator of non-self.

"O all of you, listen as this sūtra, established by the Sage, is being proclaimed— a destroyer of the doctrines of other schools, expressive, powerful, containing the meaning well-spoken by the Sugata, and a treasury of glory. (8.1.29) Thus [he said].

§1 Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus, in a market town of the Kurus named Kalmāṣadamya. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, I shall teach you the Dharma. I shall proclaim the holy life that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, entirely complete, perfectly pure, and purified—namely, the Brahma-faring."

That is to say, the Dharma discourse named "Ultimate Emptiness. Listen to it; attend to it well and thoroughly, and I shall speak. §2 What is the Dharma discourse on Ultimate Emptiness? Monks, when the eye arises, it does not come from anywhere; when it ceases, it does not go to any accumulation. Thus, monks, the eye comes into being after not having been, and having been, it passes away. Karma exists, and its maturation exists, but an agent is not apprehended.
It is that which casts off these aggregates and links with other aggregates, and nothing other than this conventional designation of phenomena.

"Monks, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind, when arising, do not come from anywhere; when ceasing, they do not go to any accumulation. Thus, monks, the mind, having not been, comes to be; and having been, it passes away. There is karma, there is its ripening, but no agent is found who casts off these aggregates and reconnects with other aggregates, except for the conventional designation of phenomena."

In this regard, this is the conventional designation of phenomena (*dharmasaṃketa*): namely, "when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. That is to say: conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces (*saṃskāra*); conditioned by the formative forces is consciousness (*vijñāna*); conditioned by consciousness is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); conditioned by the six sense bases is contact (*sparśa*); conditioned by contact is feeling (*vedanā*); conditioned by feeling is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); conditioned by craving is grasping (*upādāna*); conditioned by grasping is becoming (*bhava*); conditioned by becoming is birth (*jāti*); and conditioned by birth is...
From this, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair arise; thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.

§5 That is to say: when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is to say: from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness; from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; from the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases; from the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact; from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; from the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; from the cessation of clinging...

With the cessation of existence, there is the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair cease. Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering. This is called the Dharma discourse named "Emptiness in the Ultimate Sense."

"Monks, I shall teach you the Dharma. I shall proclaim the holy life (*brahmacarya*) that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, both in meaning and in phrasing; which is entirely complete, pure, and radiant. That is to say, it is the discourse on the Dharma named 'Ultimate Emptiness' (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). This is what was said in response to what I had spoken. The Blessed One said this: "In whatever way the mind-form (*manorūpa*) moves toward an object—whether it be unstable or indeterminate—it grasps that object and proceeds accordingly."
The ignorant person binds the heart with such intense sufferings;
for the grasping at a self, constructed falsely, brings misery to living beings.
Here, there is neither an agent nor even an experiencer.
This body is carried along without an owner;
listen, O best of listeners, to how the river of saṃsāra flows as it is being described. 8.3.2
Dependent upon the six sense-faculties and the six objects of the senses,
the sixfold consciousness arises.
The process of contact operates with respect to these three, from which proceeds the activity of memory, cognition, and action. (Buddhacarita 16.89)
Just as fire is produced through the conjunction of a gem, fuel, and the sun by way of a logical necessity,
so too [the fire of consciousness] arises from the dependence upon the elements, the objects of the senses, and the sense-faculties.
Purposeful actions depend upon human agents.
Just as, indeed, a sprout is born here from a seed, so too... *Buddhacarita* 16.90.

Nor is that which is the seed the sprout; nor is it elsewhere than from that, nor is it that very same thing. Thus, the sequence [of the self] does not proceed from the body, the sense faculties, or the intellect. (8.3.5)
If the body were independent in its performance of actions, it would carry out its functions even without the sense organs and the mind.
But when there is nothing at all apart from intellect and the other [faculties], therefore this entity consists solely of a collection. (8.3.6) *Buddhacarita* 16.92

As long as the ocean remains fierce with the tumultuous roar of its agitated waters, tossed and splashed by waves crowded with sea-monsters, crocodiles, and sharks moving restlessly like ripples on the surface;
and as long as Mount Meru stands with its body embraced by the rays of the constellations, the moon, and the hosts of planets.
"May the teaching of the Friend of the Three Worlds, who possesses the strength of the ten powers, blaze forth as long as there are beings here [in this world]. Thus it should be recited. (8)
Whatever beings have gathered here, whether standing upon the earth or in the atmosphere,
let them always maintain loving-kindness toward all creatures and practice the Dharma by day and by night.
